stem: A non-dividend-paying share trades at USD 75. A six-month European put with an exercise price of USD 70 costs USD 2.10, and the annual risk-free rate is 4%. Using put-call parity, the price of a six-month European call with the same exercise price is closest to:

rationale.B: Incorrect. 7.10 uses the undiscounted exercise price of 70.
rationale.C: Incorrect. 4.26 = 75 − 2.10 − 68.64 subtracts the put price instead of adding it.

stem: The one-year forward price of an asset is USD 105. A one-year European call on the asset with an exercise price of USD 100 costs USD 9.00, and the annual risk-free rate is 3%. Using put-call-forward parity, the price of a one-year European put with the same exercise price is closest to:

rationale.A: Incorrect. 4.00 = 9 − 5 fails to discount the difference between the forward price and the exercise price.
rationale.C: Incorrect. 13.85 adds the discounted difference instead of subtracting it; when F0 > X, the call is worth more than the put.

stem: A synthetic European put can be created by:
options: buying the underlying, buying a call and borrowing the present value of the exercise price
writing a call, buying the underlying and lending the present value of the exercise price
buying a call, short-selling the underlying and lending the present value of the exercise price
explanation: From parity, p0 = c0 − S0 + X/(1 + r)^T: buy the call, short the underlying and buy a risk-free bond (lend) worth the PV of X.

rationale.A: Incorrect. This combination has the wrong signs on the underlying and the bond.
rationale.B: Incorrect. Writing a call and buying the underlying is a covered call; adding a bond does not create a put, because the call and underlying signs are reversed.
rationale.C: Correct. Long call, short underlying and long bond replicates a long put.

stem: A non-dividend-paying share trades at USD 40. One-year European options with an exercise price of USD 40 are quoted at USD 4.50 (call) and USD 3.20 (put). The annual risk-free rate is 5%. The riskless profit per share available today from exploiting the mispricing is closest to:
explanation: Parity put = 4.50 − 40 + 40/1.05 = 2.5952. The market put of 3.20 is overpriced. Write the put and buy the synthetic put (buy call, short share, lend 38.0952): 3.20 − 4.50 + 40 − 38.0952 = 0.60.

rationale.A: Incorrect. 1.30 = 4.50 − 3.20 assumes the parity put equals the call price, which ignores discounting the exercise price.
rationale.B: Incorrect. 2.60 is the parity value of the put, not the arbitrage profit.
